title: The Bayeux Tapestry is not a tapestry: it is nearly 70 metres of embroidery

cover.alt: A scene from the Bayeux Tapestry: embroidered knights on horseback and soldiers with shields and spears beneath the Latin words of the death of King Harold.

body: The Bayeux Tapestry tells the story of the Norman conquest of England in 1066 on a strip of linen nearly **70 m long** and about 50 cm tall. It is not a woven tapestry at all: the scenes were stitched in wool yarn onto a linen ground with stem stitch and couched laid work, so technically it is an embroidery. It was probably made in England, most likely around Canterbury, in the decades after 1066, and is generally thought to have been commissioned by Bishop Odo of Bayeux, William the Conqueror’s half-brother. It is first recorded in a 1476 inventory of Bayeux Cathedral, and its final scenes are lost.

slides.alt: Scene 32 of the Bayeux Tapestry: a group of men point up at a comet with a streaming tail embroidered in the upper border, beside the Latin caption about the star.
slides.caption: Scene 32: men point at a comet in the border, the earliest known picture of Halley’s Comet, which appeared in 1066.

slides.heading: Which appear most often on the tapestry?
slides.note: Plus 37 buildings and fortifications, and Latin captions naming people and places.
slides.explanation: Animals win: 994 of them, mostly in the borders, against 623 people, 438 plants and 41 ships.

left.label: A tapestry
left.text: Woven on a loom: the picture is built into the cloth itself as coloured weft threads cross the warp.

right.label: This one
right.text: Coloured wool stitched onto finished linen, with stem stitch for outlines and couched laid work for fills. So the famous ‘tapestry’ is an embroidery.

slides.heading: Who made it, and where
slides.text: The old French tradition tied it to Queen Matilda, William the Conqueror’s wife, but that is legend. 20th-century scholars concluded that Bishop Odo of Bayeux commissioned it; he appears in it four times. Most now think it was stitched in England, probably at Canterbury, perhaps by 1077 for the cathedral’s dedication.

slides.question: What happened to the end of the tapestry?
options: It was sewn on in the 1800s
It was left as blank linen
slides.explanation: The final scenes are lost. The last caption, ‘and the English turned in flight’, is a later addition that scholars reject as spurious.

events.text: Events shown: the Norman conquest, Harold to Hastings
